land.text: the Tang realm Zhu Wen governed: 'By 904, Zhu had gained control of both Tang capitals, Chang'an and Luoyang'

predecessors.note: Zhu Wen had Emperor Zhaozong murdered in 904 and deposed Emperor Ai in 907-908 (Later Liang page); the Later Liang is the Tang's successor in the central plain.

land.text: the Later Liang realm, taken by Li Cunxu in 923

successors.note: Li Cunxu 'destroyed Later Liang in 923 and founded Later Tang'. The Later Liang infobox also lists Jie Yan and Zhao as successors: both are earlier regional states, not heirs to Later Liang land. The north bank of the Yellow River had passed to Jin (later Tang) in 915-916.

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe for 907 alone (Cliopatria starts Later Liang in 911, four years after the 1 June 907 founding). Cliopatria's 911 shape carried back, because the Later Liang page says the state 'controlled most of northern China' without dating a change before 915, but with two cuts from the Li Maozhen page: Baoda (保大) and Baosai (保塞), 'headquartered in modern Yan'an', were Qi's until late 908 (all 97 cells of the Yan'an disc lie inside Cliopatria's Later Liang shape), and Jingnan (靜難, 'headquartered in modern Xianyang') was Qi's until Li Baoheng 'surrendered Jingnan Circuit to Later Liang' in 915 (42 of the 55 cells of the three Jingnan discs lie inside it). The Later Liang page gives no area and no province list; Zhu Wen's 907-911 conquests are not on any opened page (the Zhu Wen page says only that 'most circuits around the former Tang realm reacted to the transition by submitting to the new emperor's authority'), a bridging judgment. fx-29 (F145): Jin's Shanxi cut from the shape. Cliopatria's Later Liang outline holds 526 of the 798 Shanxi cells, 385 of them inside the Jin dossier's Shanxi, but the Later Liang page says Shanxi 'controlled by Shatuo Turks state Jin' 'remained largely outside Later Liang control' and the Jin page says that in 907 Jin 'consisted of most of Shanxi' with 'Linfen, Hezhong, Jincheng, Qinyang' taken by Later Liang; what stays is the Linfen, Hezhong and Jincheng discs.

keyframe_review.note: Valid for 911-914 only. Cliopatria keeps this outline (793,636 km2: Henan 95 percent, Shandong all, Hubei 54 percent, Shaanxi 48 percent, Hebei 54 percent, Shanxi 66 percent) to 921 and has Bin and Ning inside it, but the Li Maozhen page has the Jingnan Circuit under Qi until Li Baoheng surrendered it to Later Liang in 915, so the three Jingnan discs are cut for 907-914. The Later Liang page says Shaanxi was Qi's, Hebei Yan's and Shanxi Jin's and 'remained largely outside Later Liang control'; Cliopatria already leaves their own cells out. The rest of the outline for 911-914 is Cliopatria's and unverified: the Zhu Wen page lists no territory for 907-912 beyond 'most circuits around the former Tang realm' submitting. fx-29 (F145): Jin's Shanxi cut from the shape. Cliopatria's Later Liang outline holds 526 of the 798 Shanxi cells, 385 of them inside the Jin dossier's Shanxi, but the Later Liang page says Shanxi 'controlled by Shatuo Turks state Jin' 'remained largely outside Later Liang control' and the Jin page says that in 907 Jin 'consisted of most of Shanxi' with 'Linfen, Hezhong, Jincheng, Qinyang' taken by Later Liang; what stays is the Linfen, Hezhong and Jincheng discs. fx-29 (F145): the keyframe had no from/to, so the compiler took the shape's Cliopatria span (911-921) and kept this outline alive when the 915 and 916 keyframes began, which re-claimed Jin's Shanxi and the Tianxiong disc (the 915 and 916 conflicts); from 911 to 914, as this note says.

The north bank follows in 916. fx-29 (F145): Jin's Shanxi of 913 cut (Jin page: 'In 912, Jin took over Jincheng'); Jin's Shanxi cut from the shape. keyframe_review.note: New keyframe for 916-921: the land north of the Yellow River goes to Jin ('By fall 916, nearly all of the Later Liang territory north of the Yellow River had fallen to Jin'; Tianxiong surrendered 915; Yangliu fort taken 917). Hebei, Shanxi, Beijing and Tianjin are cut as a whole province-level reading, and so is Henan north of the river (Anyang, Hebi, Xinxiang, Jiaozuo, Puyang; 145 cells, about 28,700 km2, all inside Cliopatria's Later Liang shape), because the page's own Wei Prefecture (衛州, 'in modern Puyang, Henan') held a Jin garrison until Dai Siyuan's surprise attack. The Tianxiong disc is cut too, so that its Shandong and Henan cells agree with the 915 loss. Shandong north of the river is kept: no page names a town there.

keyframe_review.note: Valid for 922-923 only (the dynasty ended on 19 November 923; Cliopatria draws it to 925, which belongs to the Later Tang). Same as 916-921 plus Wei Prefecture (衛州, 'in modern Puyang, Henan'), where Dai Siyuan 'surprise[d] the Jin garrison there, capturing it', which 'allowed Later Liang to regain its foothold north of the Yellow River'. Zhaoyi and the loss of Yun Prefecture come as 923 events in the ledger. region.text: Kaifeng and Luoyang, Zhu Wen's two capitals

ledger.note: 907: Zhu Wen proclaims the Later Liang. 'Zhu Wen declared himself emperor of the new Later Liang in Kaifeng in 907'; infobox 'Established: 1 June 907', capital Luoyang 907-913. The page gives the cities, not a boundary.

region.text: the Baoda (保大) and Baosai (保塞) circuits, both headquartered in modern Yan'an

ledger.note: Late 908: Baoda and Baosai surrender to Later Liang. 'The Baosai officer Gao Wanxing (高萬興) ... and the Qi military governor of Baoda, Li Yanbo (李彥博), both surrendered to Later Liang'; Baoda is '保大, headquartered in modern Yan'an' and Baosai '保塞, headquartered in modern Yan'an'. The page gives no month; the Yan'an disc is a reading of the two circuits.

912: Jin takes over Jincheng. 'In 912, Jin took over Jincheng.' (Jin page); the same page lists 'Linfen, Hezhong, Jincheng, Qinyang' among the commands 'taken by Later Liang'. The page names no month. Mirror of former-jin /ledger/1 (added by fx-29).
913: the capital passes from Luoyang to Kaifeng (Daliang) under Zhu Youzhen. Infobox 'Kaifeng (913-923)'; the Zhu Youzhen page: he 'moved the capital to Daliang and took the throne there'.

region.text: the Jingnan Circuit (靜難), the Bin, Ning and Qing prefectures

ledger.note: 915: the Jingnan Circuit comes over from Qi. 'In 915, Li Jihui's adoptive son Li Baoheng (李保衡) killed Li Yanlu and surrendered Jingnan Circuit to Later Liang' (Jingnan '靜難, headquartered in modern Xianyang'); Zhu Zhen 'made his general Huo Yanwei the new military governor of Jingnan' and Qi never regained it. The page does not name the prefectures: Bin, Ning and Qing are the circuit's three prefectures, drawn as three 40 km discs.

915: Tianxiong goes over to Jin. 'The Tianxiong soldiers mutinied after the circuit was split, and Zhang Yan decided to surrender the circuit to Jin.' The page does not locate it; Tianxiong (Weibo) is read as the Wei Prefecture country round Daming, which is not in the gazetteer.

union.text: Henan north of the Yellow River (Anyang, Hebi, Xinxiang, Jiaozuo, Puyang)

region.text: the Later Liang cells north of the Yellow River: Hebei, Shanxi, Beijing, Tianjin and Henan north of the river

ledger.note: 916: the north bank of the Yellow River goes to Jin. 'By fall 916, nearly all of the Later Liang territory north of the Yellow River had fallen to Jin.' The page names no towns beyond Tianxiong (915); the region is the Cliopatria shape's Hebei, Shanxi, Beijing and Tianjin cells plus Henan north of the river (Anyang, Hebi, Xinxiang, Jiaozuo, Puyang: 145 cells, about 28,700 km2), a reading. The Wei Prefecture (衛州, 'in modern Puyang, Henan') of the 921-922 paragraph held a Jin garrison, so Henan's north bank had passed to Jin.

region.text: the lower Yellow River, the frontier between Later Liang and Jin

ledger.note: 917: Jin crosses to the south bank. 'Jin forces attacked and captured the border fort of Yangliu', south of the Yellow River; fighting along the river follows (Huliu Slope 919, Zhongdu 923).

region.text: Wei Prefecture (衛州, in modern Puyang, Henan)

ledger.note: 922: Later Liang regains Wei Prefecture. The Zhu Youzhen paragraph that opens 'In 921, Li Cunxu's major ally Wang Rong ... was assassinated' goes on: 'During Jin's campaign against Zhao, the new Later Liang supreme commander Dai Siyuan was able to attack Wei Prefecture (衛州, in modern Puyang, Henan) and surprise the Jin garrison there, capturing it', which 'allowed Later Liang to regain its foothold north of the Yellow River and greatly recover in its morale'. The page dates the attack to neither 921 nor 922 (the Zhao campaign ended when Zhang Chujin fell 'late 922'), so 922, the window's end, is the year given. The earlier version drew Daming (Tianxiong's 魏州), a different Wei.

923: the Zhaoyi circuit comes over from Li Cunxu's Jin. 'In spring 923, Li Jitao submitted his circuit to Later Liang' (Zhaoyi, 昭義, 'headquartered in modern Changzhi, Shanxi'; Li Cunxu had renamed it Anyi), and Zhu Zhen 'commissioned him as full military governor and renamed the circuit Kuangyi'. The land came out of Jin (the future Later Tang), not from a state of its own, so the counterpart is former-jin; Li Jitao is the defector.

region.text: Yun Prefecture, capital of Tianping Circuit

ledger.note: 923: Li Siyuan takes Yun Prefecture, Tianping's capital. 'Capturing Tianping's capital Yun Prefecture (Yunzhou)'; the page gives the year only. Yun is read as the western Shandong country round Tai'an.

region.text: the lower Yellow River, the frontier between Later Liang and Jin

ledger.note: 923: the war on the Yellow River ends with the fall of Kaifeng. Infobox 'Surrender of Kaifeng: 19 November 923'; the Later Tang page puts the Later Tang's founding in May 923 (the counterpart is Jin, which became the Later Tang).

region.text: the Later Liang realm as Cliopatria draws it for 922

ledger.note: 923: Li Cunxu takes the Later Liang realm. 'Li Cunxu, son of Li Keyong, destroyed Later Liang in 923 and founded Later Tang'; Zhu Youzhen ordered Huangfu Lin to kill him and Huangfu then died by suicide (Zhu Youzhen page, died 18 November 923).

region.text: the Later Liang realm as Cliopatria draws it for 922

ledger.note: 923: the Later Liang ends. Infobox 'Surrender of Kaifeng: 19 November 923'. The land passes to the Later Tang; Cliopatria's 924-925 years belong to the Later Tang.

wars.name: Jin-Later Liang war

zones.text: the lower Yellow River, the frontier between Later Liang and Jin
Wei Prefecture (衛州), where Dai Siyuan regained a foothold north of the river

wars.outcome: Jin (then Later Tang) victory: Tianxiong 915, the north bank 916 (including Henan north of the river), Yangliu 917, Zhao 921-922, Yun Prefecture 923, Kaifeng 19 November 923; Wei Prefecture (Puyang) was surprised and recaptured by Later Liang in 921-922, and Huliu Slope (919) was 'essentially a draw'.
wars.note: The Later Liang page describes a 'tense relationship' with the Shatuo of Jin rooted in Zhu Quanzhong's rivalry with Li Keyong, with no dated battles; the dated sequence comes from the Zhu Youzhen page. Zhongdu (923): Wang Yanzhang and Zhang Hanjie captured.

wars.name: Qi-Later Liang border war

zones.text: the Baoda (保大) and Baosai (保塞) circuits, both headquartered in modern Yan'an
the Jingnan Circuit (靜難), the Bin, Ning and Qing prefectures

wars.outcome: Later Liang gains: Baoda and Baosai (Yan'an) surrender in late 908 and the Jingnan Circuit in 915 (Li Maozhen page). Qi's 910 attack on Dingnan with Jin was driven off, and Kang Huaiying garrisoned Yongping against Qi in 914 (Zhu Youzhen page).
wars.note: Second page: Zhu Youzhen (914 Yongping). The Zhu Wen page (909: Liu Zhijun's Chang'an raid retaken by Yang Shihou and Liu Xun) is silent on territory.

wars.name: Wuning rebellion and Wu intervention
wars.outcome: Wuning's commander Wang Yin 'submitted to Wu' in fear; Later Liang generals captured Xu Prefecture; no lasting border change on any opened page.

certainty.note: No treaty line is on any opened page. The Yellow River frontier of 915-923 is a river, drawn soft; the 907-914 outline is Cliopatria's, cut for Yan'an and Jingnan from the Li Maozhen page, and otherwise unverified.

notes: Cliopatria's Later Liang Dynasty row (911-925) is the Five Dynasties Later Liang (Wikipedia 'Later Liang (Five Dynasties)'), a different state from the 6th-century Liang dynasty (502-557; slug liang-dynasty, Cliopatria 510-560) and from the Di-led Later Liang of 386-403 (slug later-liang). Cliopatria gives both Later Liang rows and the Liang Dynasty row the Wikidata id Q783489, which the existing liang-dynasty dossier uses for the 6th-century state; the id here is therefore left null (Wikidata is unreachable and the right id is not guessed). No Cliopatria rows are merged. Cliopatria's two shapes are the same 793,636 / 793,832 km2 outline; the corrected 916 outline (Jingnan in, Hebei, Shanxi, Beijing, Tianjin, Henan north of the river and the Tianxiong disc out) is about 543,000 km2 (68 percent of the cells of Cliopatria's shape; the first version of this note said 733,900 km2, which was wrong: the earlier cut of Hebei, Shanxi, Beijing and Tianjin alone already left 72 percent, about 574,000 km2) and the pages give no infobox area to compare. Cliopatria runs the state to 925; it ended on 19 November 923. The Zhu Wen reign (907-912) and the early Zhu Yougui years are not covered: the Later Liang and Five Dynasties pages are silent on Zhu Wen's wars with Jin, Yan, Zhao and Qi, so the 907-910 and 911-915 outlines are Cliopatria's and unverified. Left out of the ledger because the pages cannot place them: Huguo's return to Jin in 920 (Zhu Youqian), Wuning's revolt of 914, the Yongping garrison of 914. Nominal investitures and tribute are not drawn as vassal tints because the Five Dynasties page says it 'does not describe a general vassal or tributary system': Ma Yin was 'created the Prince of Chu' in 907 (Ma Yin page, listed in southern-chu's sources), Wang Shenzhi 'recognized the new emperor' in 909 (Wang Shenzhi page, listed in min's sources), Liu Yan was 'a former Later Liang vassal' until 917 (Zhu Youzhen page) and the infobox gives Guangdong/Guangxi 913-917. A reviewer who wants them as vassal_start/vassal_end events can add them from those pages. Gazetteer names wanted: place Daming (Wei Prefecture; used as a coordinate disc), Dongping/Yun Prefecture (Tai'an used), Lu/Shangdang (Changzhi used), Yangliu fort. FIX ROUND (2026-10-19): (1) the 916 north-bank loss now also takes Henan north of the Yellow River (Anyang, Hebi, Xinxiang, Jiaozuo, Puyang; a polygon along the river intersected with Henan, 145 cells, about 28,700 km2, where the reviewer's own polygon gave 33,889 km2: the difference is the polygon, not a page; both lie inside Cliopatria's Later Liang shape) and the Tianxiong disc, which makes the 915 loss and the 916 keyframe agree for the Shandong and Henan cells of that disc; (2) the 922 foothold is Wei Prefecture (衛州) 'in modern Puyang, Henan', not Daming, at confidence 2, and the keyframe adds back only that 40 km disc; the page does not date the attack beyond the 921-922 Zhao campaign; (3) two gains from Qi that the Li Maozhen page documents: Baoda and Baosai (Yan'an) in late 908 and the Jingnan Circuit (Bin, Ning, Qing) in 915, with keyframes 907 (without both), 908-910 and 911-914 (without Jingnan) and 915 (with Jingnan, without Tianxiong); (4) the Zhaoyi counterpart of 923 is former-jin. Disagreement with the reviewer's remark in the review notes that the seat of 衛州 was historically near Weihui (Xinxiang): no opened page says so; the drawing follows the Zhu Youzhen page, whose Puyang and Weihui discs would both lie in Henan north of the river. Thin item answered: the Zhu Wen page lists no Later Liang territory for 907-912 and only dates 908, 909, 911, 912 events, so the 911-914 outline stays Cliopatria's. Gazetteer names wanted: places Bin (Binzhou, Shaanxi), Ningxian, Qingyang and Yan'an (coordinates used), and a region 'Henan north of the Yellow River' (Henei).
